_readme: Hubs for the OpenStreetMap takeaway pull. One entry per metro.
centre + radius_miles, NOT a bbox. The first eight areas were hand-drawn
downtown boxes 1.1-2.1 miles across - 166 km2 in total, across eight
cities - which was never a decision, just a first sketch that stuck. At
that size 'Seattle' meant about forty blocks. 50 miles is 156x the area
per hub and, measured 2026-08-12, takes Seattle from 1,086 named food
places to 9,765.
A 50-mile box is 1.45 degrees and Overpass will not serve that in one
piece: the COUNT alone took 76 seconds, and a wide box answers 504 - which
is how Seattle, and later New York, dropped out of entire runs. So the
ingest TILES each area into cells and merges them, and a tile that will
not answer is reported and skipped rather than losing the metro.
The place list is CACHED per area (osm_places_cache/, 30 days). A
restaurant's existence does not change weekly, and without the cache every
run re-downloaded every place in every area to examine sixty of them:
18,282 pulled from a volunteer-run service to look at 480. Adding hubs is
cheap because of that cache; it is the WEBSITE fetching, throttled by
--max-places, that costs real time.
Adding a hub is three lines. What stops this being the whole world is not
the config - see the note in the ingest header.
_brazil: Added 2026-08-28. The matrix is read from this file, so each is its own job bounded by --max-places; adding an area costs parallel runner time, not critical path. Brazil's takeaway coverage in OSM is dense and iFood links are common, but note that looks_like_ordering only knows Western hosts, so the first sweep is the measurement of how much actually qualifies.
